en: The Song of Realizing the Way at Yongjia, composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánjué of Shènsuǐ Temple in the Tang Dynasty:
Have you not seen the idle man of the Way, who has severed study and attained non-action? He does not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor does he seek the Truth.
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature;
the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
When the Dharma-body is fully realized, not a single thing exists.
The fundamental source and original nature is the true, celestial Buddha.
The five aggregates are floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness;
the three poisons are bubbles of water, vainly appearing and disappearing.
Realizing the true mark, one is free from the dharmas of self and person;
in a single instant, the karma of Avīci hell is extinguished.
Yet, if one deceives sentient beings with false speech, [the consequences are otherwise].
Having invited upon oneself the retribution of having one's tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
one suddenly awakens to the Tathāgata-dhyāna;
the six pāramitās and myriad practices are perfected within its essence.
Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear;
upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a great chiliocosm remains.
There is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain.
Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire;
for a long time, the dust-mirrored mind has never been polished.
Today, you must clearly analyze and discern it.
Who is without thought? Who is without birth?
If in truth there is neither birth nor non-birth, go call the wooden mechanical man and ask him.
Seeking the Buddha’s grace, when will your merit be perfected?
Let go of the four elements and do not grasp at them;
within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with whatever you drink and eat.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty;
this is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment.
This definitive teaching manifests the true Saṃgha.
There are those who refuse to investigate directly according to their own capacity;
they seek the root straight on, as sealed by the Buddhas.
To pluck leaves and search for branches is not what I can do.
People do not recognize the mani jewel;
it is personally obtained within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Its six kinds of divine functions are both empty and not empty.
A single orb of light, neither form nor non-form;
purifying the five eyes and attaining the five powers,
it can only be known through realization, for it is difficult to fathom.
Beholding one's form in a mirror is not difficult;
grasping the moon in water—how could it ever be seized?
Always walking alone, always stepping forth alone.
The realized ones travel together on the path to nirvāṇa;
their style is ancient and their spirit pure, so naturally lofty.
Their appearance is haggard and their bones are firm, yet people pay them no heed.
This destitute Śākya-putra claims in speech that he is poor;
yet in truth, while his body is poor, his Way is not poor.
Being poor, his body is constantly clad in coarse, tattered hemp garments.
The Way is the heart-treasury of priceless jewels;
these priceless jewels are inexhaustible in their use.
To benefit beings in accordance with their capacities, one never begrudges them.
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence;
the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground.
When the superior practitioner makes a single resolution, all is fully understood.
Those of middling and inferior capacity are mostly learned yet lack faith;
they merely strip away the soiled garments within themselves—
who could boast of their diligence to others?
Let others slander me; let others be at fault.
To carry fire to burn the heavens is but a weary toil for oneself.
When I hear this, it is as if I were drinking nectar.
Dissolving them away, one enters suddenly into the inconceivable.
Contemplate that harsh words are a source of merit;
these are what constitute my spiritual friends.
Not giving rise to enmity or kinship due to slander or defamation—
how can this manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience?
The fundamental principle is pervasive, and the teaching is also pervasive.
Concentration and wisdom are perfectly clear and bright, without stagnating in emptiness.
Not only have I alone now attained this realization;
the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.
The lion’s roar is spoken without fear;
when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains split asunder.
The fragrant elephant flees in haste, losing its majesty.
The devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy.
Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams,
they seek teachers and inquire after the Way to practice Zen.
Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, I have known that life and death are not interconnected.
Walking is Chan; sitting is Chan.
Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the essence remains serene.
Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one is ever at ease;
even if one encounters potent poison, one remains indifferent.
My Teacher met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
for many kalpas he was once the Rishi Kṣāntivādin,
undergoing birth after birth and death after death.
Birth and death drift on endlessly without fixed rest;
since awakening suddenly to the realization that there is no birth,
what sorrow or joy can there be amidst all honors and insults?
Entering deep mountains to dwell in an araṇya,
amidst towering peaks and secluded depths beneath long pines,
he sits at ease and in stillness within the home of a wild monk.
In quiet seclusion, dwelling in peace is truly serene;
upon awakening, one realizes that no effort need be exerted.
All conditioned phenomena are not like this.
Giving with attachment to signs produces the merit of rebirth in heaven;
it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void:
when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down.
To invite such things as lead to dissatisfaction in future lives—
how can they compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark,
which transcends all in a single leap and enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata?
Simply attain the root and do not worry about the branches;
it is like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon.
Since you are already able to understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, [you need not seek elsewhere].
Benefiting oneself and others never ceases;
the river moon shines as the pines are fanned by the wind.
Throughout the eternal night and the clear evening, what is there to do?
The Buddha-nature is the pearl of precepts, the seal of the mind-ground;
mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the robes upon his body.
The dragon-subduing almsbowl and the tiger-releasing mendicant’s staff.
The two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly;
this is not a mere display of form or a hollow practice.
It is the actual trace of the Tathāgata’s precious staff.
Seeking no truth and severing no delusion,
one thoroughly understands that these two dharmas are empty and signless.
They are neither signless nor empty, nor are they non-empty.
This is the true mark of the Tathāgata:
the mirror of the mind is luminously reflective and unimpeded;
vast and brilliantly transparent, it pervades the entire realm of saṃsāra.
Within the manifestation of the myriad phenomena in their arrayed reflections,
there is a single sphere of light that is neither internal nor external.
In this state of vast openness and emptiness, one brushes away cause and effect.
Vast and boundless wandering brings about calamity and misfortune;
abandoning the existent to cling to emptiness is likewise a sickness—
it is like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire.
To abandon deluded mind and grasp at ultimate truth—
the very mind of grasping and abandoning becomes artifice and hypocrisy.
Students who do not understand this employ it as their practice.
Deeply convinced that the thief is one's own son,
one squanders the wealth of the Dharma and destroys merit;
all this is due to nothing other than this mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Therefore, through the Chan gate, one brings the mind to its ultimate end;
by the power of sudden insight into non-arising,
the great man grasps the sword of wisdom.
The sharp edge of Prajñā is like a vajra flame;
it not only utterly destroys the minds of externalists,
but has long since caused the courage of the celestial Māras to fall away.
Thundering with the Dharma-thunder, he strikes the Dharma-drum;
spreading clouds of compassion, he sprinkles sweet dew.
As dragons and elephants trample through them, the moisture is boundless.
Those of the three vehicles and five natures have all awakened;
the snow mountains are rich and pure, free from any admixture.
Pure *sarpis* (clarified butter) emerges, which I constantly receive.
The single nature is perfectly interfused with all natures;
the single dharma universally contains all dharmas;
the single moon universally appears in all waters.
All moon-reflections in water are subsumed within a single moon.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature;
my nature is identical and merges with that of the Tathāgata.
The first stage encompasses all stages;
it is neither form nor mind, nor is it karma or action.
In the snap of a finger, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly realized.
A single kṣaṇa extinguishes three asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
all numerical and non-numerical categories—
what connection have they with my numinous awakening?
It cannot be disparaged nor praised;
its essence is like empty space, without shore or limit.
Without leaving its present location, it is eternally serene and profound.
Seeking it, you know it cannot be seen;
it cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished.
Within this state of unobtainability, there is simply attainment.

It proclaims the power of the Mahāprajñā;
whether it is right or wrong, humans cannot discern it;
its retrograde and forward movements are unfathomable even to the gods.
I have long practiced through many kalpas;
this is not a casual deception. I raise the banner of the Dharma and establish the fundamental tenets.
Clearly and brightly is the Buddha’s mandate: Caoqi is it.
Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the lamp;
twenty-eight generations are recorded in the West.
The Dharma flowed eastward into this land;
Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch. The transmission of the robe through six generations became renowned throughout the world.
The number of future people who attain the Way is beyond measure.
When truth does not stand, delusion is fundamentally empty;
when both existence and non-existence are cast aside, it is neither-empty nor empty.
The twenty gates of emptiness are fundamentally non-attached;
the single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical.
The mind is the faculty, and dharmas are the objects.
The two are like blemishes upon a mirror;
when the stains and impurities are entirely removed, the light finally appears.
When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, the nature is itself the truth.
Alas for this final dharma and evil age!
Sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline.
Far removed from the Sage, their false views run deep.
When the power of Māra is strong and the Dharma weak, there is much fear of harm;
upon hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s sudden (sudden) gate,
one vows to eliminate [the obstacles] so that they may be shattered like tiles.
What is created resides in the mind; the calamity returns to the body.
There is no need for grievance or complaint, nor should one lay blame on others.
If you wish not to incur karma leading to the Avīci Hell, [you must act with mindfulness].
Do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees;
it is dense, deep, and silent, where the lion dwells.
In the tranquil realm, he wanders alone amidst the forest;
the running beasts and flying birds all flee afar,
while a troop of lion cubs follows behind him.
At three years old, he was already able to let out a great roar;
if a jackal were to pursue the Dharma King,
it would be a hundred years of vain clamor by a phantom creature.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching does not tolerate human sentiment;
if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must simply strive for clarity.
This is not the mountain monk’s way of asserting self and other.
In practicing the Way, one fears falling into the pit of nihilism or eternalism.
It is neither "not" nor "is," neither "is not" nor "is not not.
To err by a hair's breadth is to lose a thousand li.
Thus, the dragon girl suddenly attained Buddhahood;
otherwise, Sunakṣatra fell into ruin at birth.
Since my early years, I have accumulated learning and inquiry.
I have also once investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and śāstras;
I distinguished names and characteristics without knowing when to cease.
Entering the sea to count its sands is but a weary toil for oneself.
Yet I was harshly rebuked by the Tathāgata:
"What benefit is there in enumerating another's treasures?
From the start you have stumbled; you have realized your conduct was in vain."
For many years I have vainly been a guest of the dusty world;
my disposition is perverse and my understanding mistaken,
for I have not attained the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching.
The diligence of the two vehicles lacks the Bodhicitta;
the cleverness of the non-Buddhists lacks true wisdom.
They are both deluded and utterly foolish.
From an empty fist, one gives rise to the false understanding that it is a real moon;
to grasp the finger as the moon is to labor in vain.
Within the phenomena of the sense faculties and their objects, one falsely fabricates strange delusions.
When not a single dharma is perceived,
one is then called Avalokiteśvara; when this is realized,
karmic obstructions are seen to be originally empty.
If one has not yet realized [the truth], one must repay former debts;
like a hungry person encountering a king's banquet who cannot eat,
or a sick person meeting the King of Physicians who fails to recover.
Practicing dhyāna amidst desire through the power of knowledge and vision,
a lotus born from fire can never be destroyed;
by courageously offering alms despite committing a grave offense, one awakens to non-arising.
Having attained Buddhahood long ago, he remains present now;
with the lion’s roar, he speaks fearlessly,
deeply lamenting those who are muddled, dull-witted, and stubborn.
They only knew that committing grave offenses would obstruct Bodhi,
yet they did not see the Tathāgata’s secret instructions for opening [the path].
There were two bhikṣus who committed sexual misconduct and killing.
Upāli’s glow of insect-like light increased his bonds of sin;
the Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled his doubts,
just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow.
The power of inconceivable liberation is as boundless as the sands of the Ganges;
I dare not decline the toil of making the fourfold offerings.
Even ten thousand taels of gold could not exhaust its value;
Though one’s bones were ground to powder and one’s body shattered, it would not suffice as recompense.
A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends billions of worlds.
The King of Dharmas, most supreme and victorious,
is realized by Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel.
Those who receive it with faith will all be in accord;
they see clearly that not a single thing exists—
neither person nor Buddha.
The trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean;
all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head.
When concentration and wisdom are perfectly clear and bright, they shall never be lost.
The sun may grow cold and the moon may grow hot,
yet no demons can destroy this true teaching.
The majestic carriage of the elephant advances in vain upon the road;
who has seen a cicada able to block its tracks?
A great elephant does not travel upon the narrow paths of a hare.
Great enlightenment is not constrained by minor details.
Do not slander the vast expanse with your narrow perspective.
Before you have realized it, I shall now give you my final parting instruction.

The Song of Realizing the Way of Yongjia; the Biography of the Great Master Wuxiang. Biography of the Great Master Wuxiang, composed by Yang Yi—Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Chao-san Dafu, serving as Left Palace Attendant, Director of the Office for Imperial Edicts, Joint Compiler of the National History, Examiner of the Historiographical Institute, Pillar of State, Marquis of Nanyang Commandery with a fief of one thousand one hundred households, and recipient of the Purple Golden Fish Bag. As for the Chan Master Xuangjue of Yongjia in Wenzhou: he was...
He was a native of Yongjia.
His surname was Dai.
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven.
He thoroughly investigated the Tripitaka to refine his understanding of the Tiantai school’s intent,
contemplating the Perfect and Wondrous Dharma-gate amidst the four modes of deportment.
He constantly immersed himself in meditative contemplation.
Later, inspired by the exhortations of Chan Master Zuo Xi Lang,
he [joined] Chan Master Ce of Dongyang.
They went together to Caoxi;
upon first arriving, he shook his staff and carried his water jar,
circumambulating the Patriarch three times.
The Patriarch said,
"Now, a śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices."
"Venerable sir, from what direction have you come that you give rise to such great conceit?
The Master replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift."
The Patriarch said:
"How can one realize non-arising?
To understand it thoroughly is the swiftest way."
It is said: "The essence is itself non-arising;
realizing that it is fundamentally without speed.
The Patriarch said:
"So it is, so it is. At that moment, there was no one in the great assembly who was not struck with amazement.
The Master, having duly assumed his dignified demeanor, paid his respects;
after a short while, he took his leave.
The Patriarch said:
"Is your return too swift?
The Master said,
"Since it is fundamentally non-moving, how could there be any swiftness?"
The Patriarch said,
"Who knows that it is not movement?
[The monk] replied, "It is you, O benevolent one, who gives rise to discrimination."
The Patriarch said,
"You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising.
He replied, "If there is no arising, how can there be a 'meaning'?"
The Patriarch said,
"If there is no intention, who is it that makes distinctions?
He replied, "Distinction itself is not intention."
The Patriarch sighed and said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Stay for one night."
At that time, he was called the "One-Night Awakened One.
Master Ce then detained the teacher,
who descended the mountain the following day and returned to Wenjiang.
Students flocked to him from all directions,
and he was titled the Great Master Zhijue.
He authored the *Chanmen wuxiu yuanzhi* (The Perfect Meaning of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School).
Arranging these from the shallow to the profound,
Wei Jing, the Regional Inspector of Qingzhou,
compiled them into ten chapters.
These were titled the *Yongjia ji* (Collected Works of Yongjia) and the *Zhengdao ge* (Song of Realizing the Way),
both of which have been widely circulated in the world. Thus it is said.
